This paper presents a enhancements to the classic Poisson Wold-Granger model, evolving it into a new variant called the TV-PAR model. The main improvements made to the original model include the ability to account for changing relationships between variables over time and the consideration of time-varying correlations between variables. A method for estimating the parameters of the model has been proposed, and the TV-PAR model's superiority over the TVAR model is demonstrated through both simulation and real-world data analysis.

Air quality monitoring requires effective and efficient techniques, especially over vast areas like states and countries. While optical data from solar measurements has been extensively used for this purpose, stellar photometry, though promising, remains largely unexplored in atmospheric research due to challenges in distinguishing its effects. However, our analysis of optical depth calculations from both solar and stellar measurements reveals that their patterns are nearly identical, allowing for the use of stellar photometry in atmospheric studies. By analyzing time-series data from three boards measuring solar radiation and three filters observing a distant star, we were able to calculate aerosol optical depths in real-time using both methods, showing almost identical results. This research demonstrates that stellar images can be utilized for atmospheric research, expanding the use of existing cameras and significantly lowering costs for air quality monitoring systems, especially in developing countries.

Molecular dynamics simulations are highly effective in replicating a given configuration of a chemical substance, yet their utility is severely constrained by the intricate nature of chemical structures and the resultant difficulty in exploring the full range of possible configurations. This limitation hampers the application of molecular dynamics, particularly in polymer science and biomolecular research, where configural changes often require substantial configurational relaxation. An alternative approach, lattice-based methods, suffers from limitations in accurately depicting chemical substances due to its discrete nature. This accuracy deficit is especially critical when studying substances with complex chemistry, such as block copolymers, where chemical asymmetries are of interest. This paper introduces an innovative lattice-free initial configurational construction technique tailored for molecular dynamics simulations, leveraging the flexibility of side-arm structures to resolve configural entanglements during dynamics simulations. This method achieves a remarkable success rate of 99.4% in bond formation for a highly asymmetric triblock polymer (A50-B2-C100), outperforming lattice-based techniques and marking the first time such a complex structure has been subject to a configurational dynamics simulation.

The development of human reference standards is recognized as a practical approach to evaluating the performance of descriptive image-based systems, yet there has been no in-depth analysis on how effective this evaluation method truly is. To bridge this knowledge gap, we conduct a comprehensive study to determine the correlation between human reference standards and the actual quality of automatic descriptions, and also explore various factors that may influence this correlation. Our research utilizes three large-scale, publicly available datasets and defines a new metric called Weighted User Agreement (WUA) to better measure the effectiveness of human reference standards in assessing image description systems. The results obtained from our analysis demonstrate that human reference standards do have a positive impact on evaluating system performance, yet there exists a significant variability in their effectiveness based on certain factors such as the prevalence of errors in the description-based system and the prevalence of conflicting human reference standards. Our findings not only contribute new insights into the evaluative process for description-based systems but also highlight the complexity of language understanding within the context of human-refereed environments.

We present a novel measure of theoretical field intricacy in a geometric context. By leveraging an exact formulation of conservation of momentum in an inviscid, inviscid fluid flow we create a kernel function for computing mutual information in an inviscid fluid field. Furthermore we create a complex-valued constitutive relationship in this geometric context that results in a set of equations identical to the generalized Euler-Arnold dynamics governing angular velocity distributions on manifolds without boundary.

In 2007, NASA's WMAP satellite produced precise measurements of the cosmic microwave background that revealed the average number of baryons in the universe with high accuracy. However, observations of large-scale structures have started to show discrepancies when compared to these precise measurements. To address this issue, various theories have been proposed that predict the existence of new low-mass particles that did not come into existence during the big bang. One such particle, if it exists, could have formed after the big bang and might be detectable through direct searches, as it could interact very weakly with known matter. If this new particle interacts even more minimally with matter, it could have been present since the big bang and contribute to the universe's structure formation, but remain undetectable through direct searches and classified as dark matter.

In our previous work, we proposed a broadband non-orthogonal waveforming technique for MRC combining of OFDM subcarriers and AMPM combining their amplitudes and phases to design efficient power systems that integrate data transmission. To reduce the complexity of optimization when optimizing this system, we in this paper introduce simpler alternative problems for its variant when using a single data stream over one or two antennas. These simpler problems, SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM equivalents, focus on optimizing data transmission through a single subcarrier under a peak transmit power constraint, effectively behaving like an integrated data and power system that utilizes broadband waveforming with one data stream over a single subcarrier.

Integrating new experimental data with existing parton distribution function (PDF) sets is an essential task in the field of high energy physics. As a theory framework, our PDF matching option enables the local adjustment of both novel and outdated experimental data on QCD processes. A key innovation of this framework is its utilization of projected data, which is treated as cross-section measurements of a hypothetical process. This allows for a consistent application of theoretical uncertainties and scale choices, as well as the generation of adjusted PDF sets that can be used for further experimental predictions. A notable example of this framework's application is provided, demonstrating its use in adjusting PDF sets with new experimental data.

Turbulent jet fires are susceptible to instability when exposed to acoustic waves, leading to intense oscillations and potential structural damage through resonance. This phenomenon is particularly relevant in industrial settings, as it can compromise the integrity of load-bearing frameworks. To better understand this interaction, we developed a linearized model that examines the reaction of a gas jet fire to acoustic disturbances. By incorporating an active flame technique, we were able to account for turbulence-flame chemistry interactions within the framework. The model's predictions were found to align with existing research, demonstrating that velocity fluctuations induced by acoustic waves can disturb the flame and generate additional heat release. This in turn causes pressure fluctuations that amplify the initial oscillations through a feedback mechanism.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a reformulation of general relativity where the Einstein-Hilbert action is based on a mobile, nonlocal average of the Ricci scalar. Previous studies have produced nonlocal to local gravity models for static gravitational fields and identified equivalences between nonlocal gravity and other modified gravity theories like $f(R)$ and exponential gravity. This article, however, is a unique rewrite of nonlocal gravity into a non-local model with a dynamic field representation, exposing a direct connection to a previous dynamic field-based exponential gravity model. The new formulation allows nonlocal gravity to remain equivalent to exponential gravity even when the metric changes locally. The article also discusses how the model can be extended to a generalised form with power-function models and highlights the theory's potential to describe large-scale universe dynamics, including its acceleration.

The LHC in its initial years will facilitate a variety of experiments within the smallest computer systems, leveraging existing infrastructure and software frameworks such as Root and HepOS. These experiments will utilize Linux-based systems with minimal resources, leveraging off-the-shelf hardware and software. A detailed description of the proposed setups is provided, along with an outline of the necessary Root scripts for data processing and a brief overview of hardware and software requirements.

Observations of some X-ray binary stars in the Galactic Centre have revealed a possible link between the masses of black holes and the existence of dormant periods. In contrast, the potential for such a dormant phase in neutron star systems has not been clearly established. This study proposes that neutron star binary systems near the Galactic Centre may experience short dormant phases following each outburst, and these dormant phases could be the source of binary systems observed in a quiet state within a specific mass range. The hypothesis suggests that these dormant phases result from a brief interruption in the outburst that creates a low-angle orbit between the neutron star and the accretion disk, similar to what is thought to occur in black hole systems. The pattern of binary systems with low mass neutron stars in a quiet state could reflect this behavior, and the outbursts of such systems might be influenced by the rotation of the neutron star, just as is the case with black hole systems. Overall, both the outburst patterns and the existence of short dormant phases in black hole and neutron star systems could be governed by the same fundamental mechanisms, leading to a similar binary mass distribution in the Galactic Centre.

Bipartite graphs are highly significant in the field of theoretical computer science. A particularly intriguing unsolved problem concerns whether a constant h exists that guarantees the polynomial-time solvability of the Splitting Vertex problem in bipartite graphs with exponential height. In contrast, we address a more manageable variation of this problem, defined for bipartite graphs where a similar but limited parameter, referred to as height, is given. Our focus is on finding a constant c and demonstrating that when the height is at most this value, a rational function algorithm can effectively solve the Splitting Vertex problem. As a specific application, we show how this algorithmic solution can be used to prove parameterized tractability of the Bisection Width problem when considering the gap between height and Bisection Width is at most this constant.

A form of low-frequency attack known as side-channel has been side-called or degenerated until now, which requires substantial computational resources to execute. This side-called degradation technique is applicable to side-channel attacks that target specific hardware metrics, such as power consumption, timing, and electromagnetic leaks, enabling them to operate in environments where those environments are not accessible. In these environments, side-channel data is not directly available, necessitating the deployment of attacks that rely on indirect observations. So far, executing these indirect side-channel attacks is challenging due to efficiency limitations, which make them difficult to execute effectively. Our proposed technique, HyperDegrade, is an automated framework that adapts side-channel attacks to environments where they are infeasible, by leveraging the side-called degradation method and targeting efficient execution. In a proof-of-concept demonstration, we utilized this framework to execute Saint, a high-performance side-channel attack on hash functions, and succeeded in compromising TangleTalk and ZigZag, secure communication protocols, within a single server environment.

The concept of unknotting a link by only utilizing local transformations is an open problem in topology that has attracted significant interest. Through the application of various transverse modifications during unknotting, it is possible to transverse-decompose a link into its constituent parts into separate unknots. While intriguing, this approach remains within the realm of theoretical topology. Our research focuses on a similar transverse-decomposition procedure, but this time, it is conducted within the confines of physical constraints. We propose a new local transverse-decomposing method, specifically designed for traditional and welded links, that results in separate unknots that have no interactions with one another. In addition to this approach, we demonstrate its effectiveness by applying it to a variety of sample links. Furthermore, we establish the validity of this transverse-decomposition method for all traditional and welded links.

In dynamic environments, the need for collaborative decision-making in robotic systems that utilize manual action plans is increasingly complex. This paper presents a novel collaborative decision-making strategy specifically designed for manual action plans to enhance the effectiveness of robotic system coordination. What makes this problem particularly challenging is its real-time and coordinated nature, which is compounded by limitations in computation, communication, and maneuver capabilities of the robots involved. The proposed collaborative policy utilizes local information to make decentralized decisions to optimize collaborative outcomes, taking into consideration the stochastic characteristics of communication failures within conventional networks. To evaluate the proposed managerial approach, a learning-based assessment method is utilized to manually analyze the outcomes, resulting in optimal parameters' identification. The findings demonstrate that the proposed collaborative policy effectively optimizes collaborative decision-making, actively learns from experienced outcomes, and significantly improves decision-making, communication, and maneuver abilities, thereby benefiting practical applications.

In our preceding work, we established that the group of symmetries for a triangular surface can be embedded within the product of Garland spaces associated with the triangular lattice's boundary. This article serves as a follow-up, presenting a comparable result for a specific class of groups. Specifically, we prove that the product of two Garland spaces constructed from a tree, corresponding to finite group representations of the lattice line, can host the group of symmetries for a bi infinite strip under certain parameter conditions. Our proof involves a novel approach, consisting of a new way to describe the bi infinite tileable strip as a specific sub-group within the product of the two Garland spaces.

The detection capabilities of interferometric gravitational wave detectors are hampered by limitations in frequency resolution, particularly in the high-frequency range. To overcome this constraint, we investigated and implemented an active control strategy for a novel configuration called the sloshing Sagnac interferometer, which involves a non-50:50 beam splitter in a Sagnac setup. By utilizing this specific arrangement, we were able to convert differential arm length fluctuations into common mode intensity fluctuations through a suspending mirror, thereby creating an additional feedback channel similar to that of a signal-recycling mirror. Through theoretical analysis and simulation, we determined that the equivalent welding distance for the new feedback loop could be set between 600m and 700m, resulting in a draft spectrum curve where the damping time constant for the mirror's thermal fluctuation was approximately 4 seconds. The model showed that the curve's limit caused by thermal noise would be similar to that of a 10m equivalent recycling loop and that the damping limit of the interferometer's curve would be overcome by the curve's shape rather than the damping limit of the mirror's thermal noise. The resulting spectrum curve suggested that the sloshing Sagnac configuration could reduce the damping time constant for thermal noise in the detector similar to that of a 100m equivalent signal-recycling loop, thereby improving the detection ability of the interferometer similar to that of an extremely lengthy equivalent signal-recycling loop without the need for a large common control

In the context of XL-MIMO systems employing stochastic access protocols, a key objective is to maximize overall data rates. Here, a novel concept, referred to as non-intersecting visible users, is introduced. These are groups of regular users, where each group is served by a distinct array of XL-MIMO antennas without any overlap in non-SI service areas between the arrays. In a specific XL-MIMO stochastic access protocol described, the overall data rate is maximized when the non-intersecting visible user groups are optimized. This optimization process is investigated through both analytical methods and simulations, revealing that in certain scenarios, systems utilizing all available arrays can achieve higher overall data rates compared to those limiting the number of active arrays.

Neural networks have largely replaced $n$-gram models in language generation due to their superior performance, yet there's not been an in-depth analysis comparing their capabilities. To fill this gap, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation of the performance of both models across 15 diverse languages, using both existing literature and our own new experiments. As a surprising finding, we observed that $n$-gram models, specifically the 4-gram variant, actually outperform neural networks when it comes to human-level performance metrics, particularly in high-resource languages. Moreover, we discovered a straightforward method to enhance the $n$-gram model's performance by incorporating its 1-gram (unigram) equivalent as a residual, leading to further improvements. As a ultimate achievement, the combined unigram-four-gram system could actually surpass the performance of the Stand-alone neural model, demonstrating the potential of unigram-$N$-gram hybrid systems in language generation.

This investigation seeks to refine the capabilities of optical symbol recognition (OSR) by incorporating pre-processing steps that leverage existing document structure and regular expressions. By integrating these prior knowledge elements, the system is designed to substantially reduce error rates, specifically in scenarios involving information extraction from structured documents. Current OSR technology, which is based on deep learning, is often hindered by its dependence on vast, annotated training datasets that mirror the characteristics of the target document. However, the refined system overcomes this obstacle by utilizing existing document structure and simple pattern-matching techniques such as regular expressions to aid in the learning process. The enhanced system, which we have dubbed iOCR, is designed to be highly accurate when the document in question contains structured information. Our evaluations, which utilized annotated datasets from the American Election Archive and a variety of publicly accessible documents, revealed that the integrated use of document structure and pattern-matching significantly improves the performance of the system. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the incorporation of simple pre-processing steps, such as font-based classification, can lead to additional performance gains. The code for our paper is available on GitHub at the following URL: https://github.com/ryan227105/iOCR

A simplified computational model of atmospheric dynamics was used to investigate the circulation patterns of terrestrial and giant planets and their moons, taking into consideration variations in factors such as rotation speed, temperature, and atmospheric composition. A broad spectrum of scenarios, ranging from extremely fast rotation rates of up to 60x that of Jupiter to very high temperatures of up to 1000K and thin atmospheric layers, were explored, as well as situations with little to no vertical temperature differences and strong vertical gradients, as well as the effects of Coriolis and centrifugal forces, Coriolis isolation, and the balance of centrifugal and gravitational forces. A diverse array of circulation patterns, including geostrophic and gradient flows, cyclostrophic and beta-drag induced turbulence, and various types of super-rotation were observed in response to these varying conditions, as well as the interaction between atmospheric layers and the effects of vertical and horizontal variations in velocity and temperature.

This study tackles two well-known integral representations, the Beta and Gamma integrals, which encounter difficulties at specific points, by developing their Bessel-type regularized alternatives. We apply these alternatives to create modified versions of the 1/Gamma function, which we find and analyze in this study.

A novel statistical framework, termed "random quantum hydrodynamics," has been developed to facilitate large-scale simulations of Bose-Einstein condensates. Within this framework, an external potential influencing a fluid's hydrodynamic behavior is treated as a random variable, allowing the underlying quantum nature of the fluid to be incorporated through the phase of the potential. This approach decouples the quantum and hydrodynamic aspects of the fluid's dynamics, enabling stable large-scale simulations. The underlying mathematical foundation employs Wigner representation of external potential and Squared-Gibbs representation of hydrodynamic behavior, with their combined evolution described by the Vlasov-type equation derived from the Liouville operator. This framework ensures positivity of the density matrix and preserves the Bose commutation relations. Moreover, it can be extended to incorporate particle-particle interactions, specifically a contact interaction modeled through a mean-field approximation.

Artificial intelligence has made significant advancements in knowledge-based systems, with the use of large-scale pre-trained models that can be adapted to various domains through efficient and cost-effective methods. One such technique is FIK, or Factorized Interval Knowledge, which plays a key role in pre-training LLMs on extensive knowledge bases. FIK consists of two parts: representing knowledge as fact intervals and describing relationships between entities and fact intervals. The FIK model can efficiently store and represent vast knowledge bases, support various knowledge representation needs, and enable the model to learn and infer knowledge-based information. FIK's contribution to pre-training LLMs on massive knowledge bases is significant, with demonstrated improvements in the efficiency of knowledge pre-training, the capacity to represent diverse knowledge structures, and the performance on inference tasks.
We present an concise overview of the AMP framework, focusing on its core mathematical principles.

A generalization of the $sl_2$ algebra, the $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ algebra, is a higher rank algebra that plays a significant role in mathematical physics and combinatorics. For the Racah algebra, a well-known mathematical structure, we derive explicit formulas for its generators and establish its connection to the $Z_4(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ algebra. Moving on to the $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ algebra for $n \ge 4$, we present the defining relations and reveals its mathematical properties. Additionally, we obtain a recursive formula for the dimensions of the $n$-th graded component of the $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ algebra's algebra of grades and link this sequence to combinatorial structures such as diagonal and monomial matchings in polygons.

Paired tests play a significant role in structured test indicators such as PE and PP, thus their reliability is crucial, necessitating a reliable way to evaluate changes between model iterations, thus paired paired-permutation tests are used to ensure improvements are not coincidental, thus their effectiveness is guaranteed, thus their significance is ensured. To make this test more effective, especially in deep learning contexts, a theoretical foundation is needed, thus a precise definition of paired-permutation testing is established, thus its effectiveness is guaranteed, thus its significance is ensured. In a particular context, a quick way to determine the relationship between various model indicators is used, thus a hierarchical framework for paired tests is presented, thus its effectiveness is guaranteed, thus its significance is ensured. A specific context, a method to determine the relationship between various model indicators is used, thus a paired-permutation test is conducted, thus the results are analyzed, thus the context is discussed in both, a context discussion and a conclusion are drawn in a structured test report on structured test indicators.

Following the framework of PMD, we investigate the triangular flow $v_3$ in heavy ion collisions to determine its connection to initial centrality and its role in establishing an isotropic velocity pattern. Utilizing NJOY data, we centrate Au+Au and Cu+Cu collision configurations at 20 GeV nucleon energy for our simulations. Our findings demonstrate that in both collision types, $v_3$ exhibits an alignment with initial centrality, with the degree of this correlation varying between collisions. Additionally, our results indicate that in Cu+Cu and the less massive Au+Au collisions, $v_3$ and its rate of change initially increase before peaking and declining, in contrast to the consistent growth observed in Au+Au collisions. We also explore the connection between angular flow polarization and initial centrization, as well as the relationship between triangular flow and particle production, revealing similar trends across all collision scenarios examined.

This study develops a predicted representation of the probability density function within a multi-target tracking scenario, characterized as a set of points on a lattice structure within infinite-dimensional space. A novel stochastic assumption on target birth dynamics is introduced, where new targets emerge either in a deterministic position or at arbitrary, unpredictable locations. A filtration concept is also defined, relating lattice-based targets to those detected by sensors, and a corresponding filter estimator is derived. The proposed lattice-based birth model offers an enhanced comprehension of target birth processes, opening up new avenues for research on optimal sensor allocation and resource management strategies.

The dynamic and unpredictable nature of soccer matches presents a significant challenge for developing a successful automatic strategy generation system. In high-stakes situations such as tied matches with a large amount of time elapsed, the need for a more context-aware strategy recommendation becomes particularly critical. Although the unique characteristics of these scenarios could theoretically lead to a noticeable win rate improvement, the specificity of each situation makes this difficult to achieve. The proposed solution involves a personalized goal scoring pattern analysis, which takes into account the ever-changing game state that includes a variety of influential factors. To achieve this, a deep reinforcement learning model was utilized, and to promote a faster learning process and better generalization capabilities, a suite of sophisticated techniques such as action embedding, curriculum learning, and off-policy learning were also employed. The results of a curriculum-built simulation with a 90x90 field and 100 players per team demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, which leads to a significant improvement in goal-scoring performance in goal-range learning and overall decision-making compared to a baseline random policy. The outcomes also suggest that the use of the current dataset might be insufficient for further performance enhancement. To address this, a proposed environment upgrade with an expanded dataset of 300 players per team and a larger 110x110 field is suggested, which is anticipated to unlock even more promising outcomes.

The emergence of structural health monitoring technology has led to large-scale engineering projects, presenting challenges in addressing complex structures like bridges with laboratory-grade single-point laser Doppler vibrometers. This study proposes a method to obtain two-dimensional surface vibration measurements using a single-point LDVS from a remote location, leveraging a real-time control system. By employing a 2x2 matrix controller that integrates a 2D scanning motion and a 50kHz data acquisition rate, we achieve a resolution of approximately 0.5cm^2 on a 1m x 1m area. The proposed system's efficacy is validated through sine sweep testing and applied to a real-time experiment, demonstrating its potential for large-scale engineering applications.

We provide an alternative derivation of the spectral non-degeneracy, as well as prove the linear and orbital stability, for a specific configuration of the Klein-Gordon equation coupled to an anharmonic oscillator. This particular setup involves a specific Hamiltonian operator representing a field $\phi$ on the real line, interacting with an anharmonic oscillator at a specific point $x=0$.

In studies of charmless $D(s)$-meson decay, two theoretical predictions, although based on different physical processes, align well with current experimental data. A specific combination of parameters, including the coupling strengths of photons and $D(s)$-mesons, as well as their decay energies, can simultaneously satisfy both the decay modes of $D$ and $D(s)$-mesons, as well as baron violation constraints. However, achieving $K-\bar{K}$ meson oscillation constraints requires a significantly lower triangle moment for $D(s)$-mesons. On the other hand, if we consider the decay of barons or the production of $D(s)$-mesons in ultra-high-energy collisions, a specific relationship is found between the decay lengths of $D(s)$-mesons and the parameters defining their anomalous behavior. Given the close mass of $D(s)$-mesons to that of $K$-mesons, it is proposed that either an enhanced decay rate of $D(s)$-mesons due to parametric resonance with $K-\bar{K}$ oscillations or a significant $D(s)$-meson displacement from the collision point could be detectable in near-future experiments.

This study explores the results of applying contextualized language models to investigate changes in semantic meaning following grammatical alterations in input sentences. So far, findings from experimental data on various grammatical modifications reveal that grammatical alterations can result in shifts in meaning, and contextualized language models are capable of detecting these alterations. Furthermore, findings from additional experiments reveal that contextualized models outperform both syntactic and contextualized grammatical rules in identifying changes in meaning resulting from grammatical alterations.

Active galactic nuclei, including quasars, have been shown to exhibit variable behavior over time. While the source of this variability is often attributed to the variability of the central supermassive black hole, another possibility exists where variability is caused by the interaction between the black hole and surrounding fields, particularly in the context of superradiance. By collecting and analyzing the spin data of 146 massive quasars, a correlation was found between black hole mass and spin, with a Spearman's rank correlation coefficient of 0.24 and a p-value of 0.01. Leveraging this spin-mass relationship, the mass range of ultra-light scalar, vector, and tensor particles that could be explained by observed variability in quasars through superradiance was determined to be 10^-22 to 10^-16, 10^-14 to 10^-8, and 10^-12 to 10^-6 GeV, respectively, leaving a remaining viable range of 10^-16 to 10^-12 GeV for axions, as other processes limit axion dark matter halo formation through superradiance. Additionally, the interaction cross-section between massive quasars and ultra-light particles, including axions, was estimated.

Quantized systems such as the harmonic oscillator are often used to illustrate key concepts in theoretical physics, including when to employ commutators or integral operators like the propagator. We present a specific calculation of the harmonic oscillator's non-equilibrium propagator that takes into account time-dependent forces, including oscillating forces, without relying on standard textbook derivations. Instead, we utilize innovative numerical methods, specifically a discrete model of the harmonic oscillator combined with Monte Carlo path integral calculations to compute the propagator.

Introducing a quantum relational Hoare logic framework, we've expanded the classical relational hyperproperty concept to the quantum domain and integrated it with the relational proof rule system for quantum Hoare logic to establish a robust verification method for quantum programs. This method enables the demonstration that certain quantum programs not only transform the pre- and post-states such that one is less than or equal to the other, as is typically required, but also induce specific measurements that certify this condition post-execution. This certification, which occurs without revealing sensitive information about the pre- and post-states, leverages the concept of localized, passive actions within the framework, which we've also defined in this context.

The accurate determination of a vector magnetic field's orientation is pivotal in formulating reliable models of magnetic field dynamics. However, as the field's inclination approaches a perpendicular stance relative to the line of sight, significant uncertainty arises in calculating the field's polarization rotation, leading to potential biases in inferred values. This situation poses a challenge when analyzing vector magnetic field data on a solar surface. We propose that this problem manifests a form of inequity, disproportionately impacting weaker magnetic field concentrations, and suggest that it's crucial to address this bias, particularly in research investigating magnetic field structures. We draw upon observations from the Spanish Integral Vector Magnetograph instrument to demonstrate that the derived field measurements from inversions exhibit this inclination-sensitive bias, noting its correlation with field strength. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a correction algorithm based on laboratory-measured properties of radio waves, proving its effectiveness in mitigating the bias. As an alternative, we also discuss the possibility of compensating for this effect by adjusting the input data for vector magnetic field models.

A lattice is considered a boolean lattice when it meets the conditions for a modular lattice and satisfies the covering property for diagonal elements, according to a result by Gr\"atzer and Weakley. Building upon this, we define a boolean lattice as an modular lattice that satisfies the same condition and a specific structural configuration known as the $B_{2,3}$-pentagon configuration. Our work generalizes the results by Gr\'atzer and Weakley, and also confirms a conjecture by Anderson, thereby establishing that our defined boolean lattice structure actually creates a boolean vector space.

A space curve whose principal normal lines at corresponding points intersect along a fixed manifold is described as a Bertrand curve, with the manifold being the envelope of those normal lines. If that manifold is timelike and the curve itself is also timelike, the curve is referred to as a Bertrand curve when the manifold is an applicable curve. This article introduces a new type of curve, the timelike Bertrand curve, within four-dimensional space-time manifolds, defining its characteristics and deriving its geometric invariants.

The machine learning community has widely adopted convolutional neural networks, particularly in image classification, with contributions from various groups playing a significant role. A notable paper by Song et al. (10) points out the deceptive nature of using alternative loss functions, such as the $l_1$-norm instead of the usual $l_2$-norm in squared error, or $log$-norm in classification problems, arguing that these changes can lead to poorer model performance. We disagree with this conclusion and aim to investigate the source of these findings, specifically exploring how altering the definition of error in a neural network's objective function, without modifying the accuracy metric (which is usually based on correct predictions), can impact the performance of deep learning models. Our research reveals that modifying the loss function's definition, and thus the priority given to misclassified images with greater or lesser confidence, has a significant effect on the model's performance, arguing that the improvements demonstrated by Song et al. are a consequence of this shift in focus, not a genuine enhancement in the accuracy of the neural network.

This study has developed an all-encompassing repository of machineshared semantic representations, named ATOMIC: An Atlas of a MachineCommon Knowledge Base consisting of Discrete Relational Concepts.With this structured knowledge framework, subsequent inference tasks canbe effectively addressed by intelligent agents.In contrast to prior knowledge graphs that consist of fixed facts about entities, ATOMIC comprises discrete relational categories along with their corresponding examples, totaling 128 specific concepts organized into 12 distinct groups.To validate the comprehensiveness of this knowledge base, inference techniques were evaluated through experimentation.On a test dataset of 2060 scenarios presented in an if-then format: behavior without given information, exhibited behavior with given information, ideal inference without learning, and generated behavior mimicking learning, various artificial intelligence models including rule-based, probabilistic, and deep learning approaches were assessed.According to the results, artificial intelligence models leveraging the ATOMIC knowledge framework demonstrated significantly enhanced inference capabilities.Artificial Point Cloud models based on Simple Point Cloud models achieved an accuracy rate of 81.1%, Simple Text models on If-Then descriptions of behavior reached 67.1%, and Simple probabilistic models attained the highest accuracy rate of 87.1%, compared to 27.6%, 36.5%, and 40.4% without the knowledge framework respectively

The field of video forecasting has seen a surge in activity, with over 300 research papers explored, and we introduce a fresh approach that outperforms existing methods. Our proposed model, that of a dual representation consisting of a graph and a matrix, has enabled a significant improvement in performance, with state-of-the-art results achieved. We've also seen a substantial reduction in computational complexity, making real-time processing of high-definition videos possible. Our decision tree-based forecasting method on the graph representation and auto-regressive approach on the matrix representation have proven to be highly effective, and we've observed that pre-processing videos to extract a low-rank matrix before forecasting leads to better outcomes.

A finite graph is considered resolution efficient when its isomorphism state can be determined by a collection of points, allowing each point in the graph to create a distinctive path sequence to every other point in that collection. This collection of points is known as the metric dimension of the graph, which is a widely studied characteristic in mathematical research. A variant of this feature, called the shortened metric dimension, is defined in this paper, allowing a certain path sequence around a point to be created, where the destination of the sequence is considered distinct from the starting point. The benefits of this modification are seen in various real-world applications such as robot mapping and sensor networks. In this research, the definable properties of the definable characteristics are identified as follows: the minimum and maximum values, as well as their corresponding occurrences, for any graph and its connected components. The equivalent state definitions are also provided for the following features: restricted traceable graphs, 2-connected graphs, and graphs lacking an isolated vertex.

Clinical settings often place stethoscopes in direct contact with a patient's chest, which can create cracking noises due to chest piece sliding or suction cup detachment, in addition to potential vibrations from the table or patient's movements. These background noises can significantly hinder the effectiveness of automated heart sound analysis systems. This research proposes combining an adaptive noise cancellation technique with a deep learning-based classifier to categorize heart sounds into four distinct categories: normal heart sound (M1) and three pathological conditions (murmurs, cracks, and drops). A convolutional neural network is employed to process the output of the noise cancellation system, taking 10-second segments of cleaned audio at a time, with a sliding window approach used to analyze the entire signal, in an effort to overcome limitations in classifying crackles. To enhance feature representation, a dilated convolution layer is incorporated into the final classification stage. To train the proposed MDCN model, a dataset of 1060 recordings was assembled, consisting of both noisy and noise-free samples of normal heart sounds and three distinct pathological conditions, as well as recordings with simulated additive interference. The results demonstrate that the combined approach significantly outperforms using either method individually, with an overall accuracy of 92.7% when applying white noise simulations at 5 times the energy level. Notably, M1, CRC, and CRD achieve accuracies of 98.5%, 95.1%, and 97.

We examine the emission of the Ci 83 and 99 micron lines in galaxies, which arises from a low-energy state of neutral iodine, distinct from its well-known fine-structure energy levels. This particular transition occurs within cold, molecular gas reservoirs, estimated to be between 10 and 30 Kelvin, where traditional line thermometry methods are ineffective. Utilizing line formation theory and molecular gas temperature data from existing studies, we discovered that the stimulated emission of this state is ineffective in generating significant emission at these temperatures. However, when temperatures rise to between 25 and 45 Kelvin, which is unusual, the line becomes observable, producing specific fluxes of approximately 0.05 to 0.1 Jy for an molecular gas mass of $10^9$ solar masses. This process could be leveraged to measure thermal profiles within cold, dense gas reservoirs in galaxies, providing insights into heating mechanisms, particularly those not directly linked to star formation, and also helping to interpret data from far-infrared surveys of galaxies.

Recent advancements in a type of particle model known as the ASEP velocity procedure are described, which is characterized by an asymmetric hopping behavior that changes based on a model-specific definition of velocity.

The global outbreak of a novel coronavirus has highlighted various mathematical models used to predict its spread. This paper aims to synthesize the diverse models into a unified understanding, emphasizing their relevance to the ongoing epidemic of a novel coronavirus. A simple compartmental model forms the foundation, with a system of differential equations describing the movement of a population between different states. To better predict real-world outbreak dynamics, several extensions to this basic model have been developed, including integrating empirical outbreak data, accounting for mask-wearing and social distancing behaviors, and considering the evolution of the novel coronavirus with new variants. Policy measures implemented to curb transmission, such as lockdowns and school closures, can be factored into the model by adjusting the rates of contact between individuals. A case study of a notable outbreak demonstrates the practical application of the enhanced model for real-world analysis.

Determining whether galactic bulges contribute to the decrease in star formation observed in massive galaxies, we analyzed a sample of 1462 nearby star-forming galaxies. We compared the spatial correlation between stellar mass and star formation rate in galaxies with and without bulges, revealing that the decline in star formation at higher masses is more pronounced in galaxies with bulges. We examined the SFR-M* relation within various radius intervals, discovering that the presence of bulges exacerbates the decline in star formation in the central regions of galaxies. We also investigated the correlation between B/T ratios and the B*-SFR* relationship, revealing that the B*-SFR* relation is more negative in galaxies with larger bulges. We examined the B*-10^0.2 * (SFR*) distribution, noting that a B/T < 0.3 is necessary for a galaxy to be classified as quiescent, with the B*-10^0.2 * (SFR*) increasing exponentially as the B/T ratio rises. Based on these findings, we concluded that galactic bulges are essential but not sufficient to explain the downturn in star formation observed in massive galaxies, likely due to a deficiency in gas supply. We suggested that the growth of bulges and the suppression of star formation in massive galaxies are driven by the same factor, likely gravitational instability in gas disks, which becomes more prevalent in massive galaxies and contributes to bulge growth in some cases.

With the rapid proliferation of social media, misinformation and fake news have become pressing concerns that demand effective detection methods. Although existing approaches have made some progress, they often fall short due to limitations in feature representation and the inability to utilize vast amounts of data for training. To tackle these challenges, we propose a novel framework called Meta-PCN, which uses a Meta-Neural Process Network to detect fake news in real-time without the need for labeled training data. In this model, a fake news instance is treated as a compromised conversation, and a meta-network is used to generate effective features for classification. To further enhance the system's performance, we also propose a pre-processor that aligns the semantic gaps between text and video components of informative videos. To evaluate the framework's effectiveness, we conducted experiments on large-scale real-world datasets, including 200+ high-profile events and 11,000+ news instances. The results show that Meta-PCN significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods, with notable improvements in detection accuracy. Additionally, we analyze the causes of errors and the behavior of counter-measures to gain deeper insights into the system's performance.

Recent advancements have seen the development of multi-level extensions of binary Golay complementary sequences, which consist of four sequences each, where pairs of consecutive sequences exhibit zero side lobe correlation. Building upon these advancements, this section describes the design of polyphase Golay complementary structures, a concept that generalizes the previous idea to sequences with multiple phases. This design strategy enables the creation of GCSs that meet specific side lobe correlation conditions, which can be tailored to fit the needs of various applications, including GCSs with the minimum possible side lobe size and those with side lobe sizes that satisfy particular conditions.

Medical imaging techniques often face challenges from malicious actions known as adversarial examples, which are difficult to detect and share with patients. There's a need for research on benign, synthetic lesions used in clinical studies, but creating them accurately is a complex task. To address both issues and the underlying difficulty in segmenting adversarial examples, a novel model called Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder (PAVAE) has been proposed and adapted for medical image processing. In its initial phase, an iterative strategy builds upon perturbed images to develop a rough segmentation of adverse lesions through multiple cycles. The model then refines this process in a secondary stage to produce more precise and subtle adversarial examples. When seeking to misclassify a given image with an adversarial approach, the first iteration's output guides the modification of the image, while the current segmentation constrains changes to the non-diagnostic regions of the brain. Evaluations show that the PAVAE model outperforms existing methods in various classification tasks on a public dataset while delivering high-fidelity results. Furthermore, the iterative tactic demonstrates superior capability in generating high-fidelity adversarial examples compared to non-iterative techniques.

Large-scale language models have been highly effective in various NLP tasks, but they fall short in understanding the nuances of natural language and excel in tasks with specific instructions, such as attribute extraction. We propose a new model, DeepContrast, designed to handle diverse attribute formats, including numerical, categorical, and boolean data, in a unified manner. By leveraging contrastive learning, our model learns to distinguish between different attribute types, enabling it to understand the structure of various attributes, such as color, size, and material, in product descriptions. Our experiments on a massive dataset, consisting of 100 million English product titles and descriptions, show that DeepContrast significantly outperforms existing models, particularly in understanding the relationships between different attributes. The results demonstrate the importance of learning the unique structure of various attributes, and the potential benefits of doing so, in e-commerce settings.

Recent advances in training extensive language models have produced high-performing models of GPT-4 and GPT-5 with over a hundred billion parameters. While these models demonstrate impressive language mastery, they often struggle with specialized tasks due to gaps in their knowledge. Retraining these models is computationally expensive and time-consuming. In an effort to bridge these knowledge gaps, we developed SKILL, an efficient framework that imparts specialized knowledge on a wide range of technical domains including machine learning, natural language processing, big data, and web development without the need for additional training. By generating high-quality explanations and constructing a multi-layered representation that captures crucial concepts and their interrelations, we managed to enhance the model's performance significantly while also significantly boosting the capabilities of base models across various technical specialized assessment benchmarks without incurring performance degradation.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between photons in vacuum, a phenomenon that allows us to examine the extension of Unruh–Liebling theorem regarding the thermal radiation of charge-nonlinear AdS black holes. In contrast to previous studies based on geometric optics, this analysis accounts for the generation of electric fields from thermal radiation, creating a feedback mechanism that influences the radiation process. As a result, a new definition of charge-nonlinear thermodynamics is proposed, in which a non-equilibrium state of black hole radiation is redefined as an equivalent equilibrium state by adjusting the mass and charge parameters of the black hole. This new definition exhibits a satisfying consistency with the principles of shadow thermodynamics and shows that nonlinear interaction leads to a more aggressive violation of the first law of black hole mechanics under non-geometric conditions. Moreover, a new definition of nonlinear response temperature is defined, which demonstrates a satisfactory analogy to the definition of Hawking temperature and displays a stronger violation of the universality of black hole event horizons' thermal properties.

Following the recently observed $B^0_d\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ mode, which is believed to be a second-order weak interaction, we have conducted additional calculations focusing on both first-order and second-order weak interaction decays of $B$ mesons that involve the production of $s$-quarks. According to CKM theory, we anticipate a minimum branching fraction of $10^{-7}$ for $B_s^0\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decays. In contrast, for $B_s^0\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decays, which are considered even more challenging, we observe a potential branching fraction in the range of $10^{-9}$ to $10^{-10}$, based on helicity suppression considerations. To enhance our understanding, we have compiled existing experimental data on the decays of $B$ mesons that produce charm and strange particles.

If a module is considered multiplicity-free under a sequence of composable algebra homomorphisms, constructing its lattice of submodules is possible by examining the lattice of subspaces for each algebra involved. This process is possible due to a theorem by Beaumont and Drobnia that establishes an isomorphism between the lattice of submodules and a join-closed subset of subspaces. In contrast, if we have a join-closed collection of modules that are analogous to subspaces, constructing the lattice of submodules is not always possible. However, an algorithm is presented that allows us to determine whether a given join-closed collection of modules forms a lattice of submodules.

We explain how to construct biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space where a specific second-order differential operator repeatedly applies, and we classify those that don't meet this criterion. Our findings reveal that having the operator recur isn't equivalent to the condition of being biharmonic, and we provide an explicit counterexample.

A 1-uniform hypergraph is a structure where a collection of edges, which are 2-element subsets of a vertex set, ensures that no two edges share more than one common vertex. This hypergraph can be represented as a fraction p/q, with q not equal to zero, when the graph formed by its edges is a collection of components, with the most significant component being a cycle of length 2m, and the remaining components being cycles of lengths 4 and cycles of length 2k (where k is greater than 1). The fraction p/q is rational in nature, and the concept of an (p/q,lambda)-identifiable code arises, in which a fraction ensures that the graph corresponding to any rational number other than p/q forms a collection of cycles of length 4 when the graph of the (p/q,lambda)-identifiable code is added to it. The term "identifiable codepoints" is used to denote the set of rational numbers (r/s) for which a graph formed by the collection of edges, representing the fraction, results in a specific structure. The article focuses on the set of all (p/q,lambda)-identifiable codepoints, denoted as I(p/q), and the purpose of determining the maximum possible value of its size, |I(p/q)|, when the number of cycles of length at least six is not greater than 1. Following recent experimental data from both LHCb and Belle II, we conduct a precise calculation of the differential decay rate for the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ transition. Initially, we compute this differential decay rate without radiative effects, then incorporate first-order QED corrections. Subsequently, we analyze the significance of form factor models that align with current data. Interestingly, we find that no single theoretical model perfectly fits the decay characteristics of $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$. However, several forms are consistent within 2 sigma, setting the stage for enhanced precision as experiments continue to accumulate more data.

When an adhesive strip is removed at a constant speed, it can cause a startling crackling sound due to material failure. As the removal speed increases, this sound's intensity and overall duration grow, potentially revealing a hidden, higher-order pattern in the force distribution along the strip's edge. This discovery of a universal, multi-scale, and time-evolving arrangement in the sound output, likely resulting from force correlations between different failure points, led to the following scaled graphs: the sound's output intensity versus the product of force drop and removal speed, and the duration of sound output versus the adhesion energy's characteristic length divided by that same product. These graphs collapsed universally across various adhesion strength levels, demonstrating a unique, scaled arrangement of failure events. This pattern was connected to a theoretical model that had previously described steady-state conditions, now extended to dynamic, non-steady environments.

In 1930, Menger developed the concept of an angle space and formulated two conjectures within this framework. The first conjecture suggested that an angle space meeting specific regularity conditions would align with a space defined by Menger, while the proposed condition for compatibility was weaker than actually necessary. A more suitable criterion was later defined in 1999. Furthermore, the first conjecture's proof relied on the sufficient condition for an angle space to be a metric space, which contained topological assumptions that were too strict. Both of these conditions were found to be too restrictive in 2002 and 2003, respectively. The second conjecture posited that the defined regularity condition was equivalent to a certain continuity property, but in fact, this condition is only necessary but not sufficient for said continuity, although a more precise sufficient condition exists. Both definitions of these properties were slightly modified in their respective criteria. Building on previous work, this paper proves that the refined continuity, regularity, and completeness conditions are equivalent to one another in angle spaces, and also establish their compatibility with the refined metric space condition, thereby fulfilling revised versions of the initial two conjectures, now redefined.

Point cloud data used in deep learning tasks often undergoes some form of initial processing, such as smoothening, to support classification and prediction tasks. The specific pre-processing method used often depends on the particular learning task being undertaken. We introduce a novel approach called Transformation-Dependent Smoothening (TPC) that dynamically adjusts the level of smoothening applied to point cloud representations based on the specific learning task at hand. Our proposed method utilizes the features extracted from a point cloud during classification and prediction tasks as a basis for determining the appropriate smoothening level. We tested our approach on three standard point cloud datasets and found that it outperformed existing methods, including cosine-based normalization, cubic smoothing, Gaussian smoothing, and baseline classification models.

The structural framework of a type-driven programming language and the geometric concepts of a higher-dimensional programming language are unified in the N-cube model, which serves as a generalization of Longest Common Subsequence and its geometric equivalent, N-Dimensional Post-Sequential Match (NPSM), used for refactoring programs safely. Within this context, derivations of equational theories are manifested as navigations through the N-cube, while program transformations are represented as transformations of the N-cube. This design facilitates the integration of geometric operations into the programming language, enabling the language to facilitate modularization of geometric proofs and vice versa. Additionally, a modularization of existing geometric proofs is demonstrated within the type system, showcasing their feasibility.

The Kummer theory generalization of $GL_2$ extends the previous $SL_2$ Kummer theory generalization, which in turn builds upon the $GL_2$ Kummer theory concept, which relies on the fundamental $SL_2$ Kummer theory, is a technique developed by Serre.

The internal structure of fiber-reinforced composites with self-sensing capabilities allows for damage monitoring by analyzing mechanical strain through electrical resistance changes in the material. While the resistance-strain relationship is linear in homogeneous materials, composites with air voids exhibit a non-linear connection due to variations in local strain and electrical conductivity. Determining the precise curve that defines this non-linear behavior is crucial for effective damage monitoring but has been challenging without detailed knowledge of the material's micro-structure. This paper presents an approach to derive the exact average resistance-strain curve for self-sensing composites with air voids by combining electrical impedance tomography, which images the void distribution, and evolutionary algorithms, which optimize the curve, based on experimental data.

This work explores a novel tensor-based interpretation of Euclidean space that aligns with classical geometric interpretations. In this representation, points in Euclidean space correspond to specific rank-2, self-dual or semi-definite tensors, while general points map to linear combinations of these tensor types. This approach yields several advantageous properties, including straightforward formulas for calculating the inner product, outer product, and norm of vectors, as well as facilitating the determination of the angle between vectors. Furthermore, it enables the derivation of Minkowski's inequality without referencing integral expressions.

The structure of right-angled Artin groups (RAAGs) associated with square-free integers is examined, with a focus on how the group decomposes under the action of dihedral subgroups. A novel, recursive definition is developed for the sets of equivalent edges within the graph underlying each integer, and it is demonstrated that this set of edges corresponds to the lattice of invariant subspaces of RAAGs. Additionally, it is proven that the lattice of invariant areas of these groups is generated by the equivalent areas defined recursively.

Recent advances in high-performance computing have led to new iterative methods for matrix inversion that outperform the classical Neumann series. We introduce three new iterative approaches, generalize previous research findings, and provide an overview of their applications in peforming matrix inversion.

Situational linear bandits is a framework applicable to a variety of real-life decisions, where the optimal choice at any given moment is determined by a high-dimensional feature space through a low-dimensional linear function. Typically, effective strategy development in this context demands an exchange of information between clients, which hampers its applicability in private scenarios. To address a more computationally efficient and privacy-preserving model known as distributed situational linear bandits, we propose a novel algorithm that achieves a better regret bound without the need for clients to exchange information. Our algorithm, named $\text{W}^2\text{-D}^2\text{-D}(\tau)$, leverages a free information source available in this particular framework, and we demonstrate that it yields improvements over prior methods, both theoretically and practically.
